title: Deceptive acts or practices (general standard)
instrument: Federal Trade Commission Act section 5, 15 U.S.C. 45, read with the FTC Policy Statement on Deception (October 14, 1983)
section: 15 U.S.C. 45(a)(1); Policy Statement on Deception, part I (Summary)
binding_note: The statute sets the standard. The Policy Statement is the Commission's own account of the elements it applies; courts have their own formulations.

in_force.note: United States Code, 2024 edition, as published on govinfo.

sources.publisher: US Government Publishing Office, govinfo (United States Code, 2024 edition)

sources.note: ftc.gov answered scripted requests with a 404 page, so the PDF was read in a browser and hashed there (79,535 bytes). Text extracted with pdf.js; line breaks normalised.

quotes.text: Unfair methods of competition in or affecting commerce, and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce, are hereby declared unlawful.

quotes.locator: Policy Statement on Deception, I. Summary, closing sentence
quotes.text: Thus, the Commission will find deception if there is a representation, omission or practice that is likely to mislead the consumer acting reasonably in the circumstances, to the consumer's detriment.

quotes.locator: Policy Statement on Deception, I. Summary, third element
quotes.text: Third, the representation, omission, or practice must be a "material" one. The basic question is whether the act or practice is likely to affect the consumer's conduct or decision with regard to a product or service.

elements.label: Likely to mislead a consumer acting reasonably in the circumstances
elements.note: This is judged from the reasonable consumer's point of view, a question for the Commission and courts.

elements.label: Material: likely to affect the consumer's conduct or decision about a product or service

does_not_prove: Section 5 is the general standard behind the more specific entries. Its two central elements, likely to mislead and material, are judgements for the Commission and courts. A match compares visible elements with the published text.
